idiom_name: boolean-returning predicates + branded flag types + strict-boolean-expressions
implementation_notes: TypeScript has no operator overloading, so the classic conversion structure cannot exist, and the checker already rejects boolean arithmetic (`true + 1` is TS2365); what replaces the classic structure is a named predicate with an explicit boolean return type (`isEmpty(): boolean`), a type predicate (`x is Valid`) when the test also narrows, and a branded flag type when two boolean-valued predicates must not be mixed. Truthiness remains: any type is accepted as a condition, so `strict-boolean-expressions` (with strictNullChecks) is the enforcement layer that reports always-truthy objects and nullable values, turning the safe-bool discipline into a lintable rule.
pitfalls: All of this is erased at runtime: the flag is a plain true/false and JavaScript coercions still apply, so the guarantee exists only while the code type-checks and lint runs.

Truthiness is allowed for non-boolean types by the checker (`if (obj)` narrows rather than errors); enable strict-boolean-expressions if the team wants boolean-only conditions, and configure it for the nullable cases they care about.
boolean is a union of true/false literals, so a widened boolean loses which question it answered - brand it when two predicates coexist.
The Boolean wrapper (`new Boolean(false)`) is an object and always truthy; use the primitive boolean and Boolean(x) only as a conversion function.
